passage: Manjula, nine, had a page of Hindi dictation words to learn, and guests were coming for dinner at eight. "I'll start when I feel like it," she told her brother Nitin at five. She drew on the back of a notebook. She helped fold napkins. She watched the pressure cooker whistle. At seven she thought, maybe now, but the doorbell rang and the house filled with cousins. By ten, when the guests left, she was yawning and the words were still unread. Amma sat with her for fifteen minutes. Manjula learnt half. In the morning, walking to school, she muttered to Nitin, "The feeling never came."

qa.q: What time were the guests coming for dinner?
qa.a: The guests were coming at eight.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she said the feeling never came?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little sheepish, realising that waiting to feel ready had used up the whole evening.

qa.q: What could Manjula try next time?
qa.a: She could start the dictation words at five before any guests arrive, even without feeling like it, since the feeling may never come.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his sister's evening?
qa.a: Nitin might find it a bit funny that she waited all evening, but also notice how tired and worried she was the next morning.

grounding: Shows a child waiting to feel like starting homework and drifting through a busy evening until it is too late.

passage: In their Kolkata flat, Kiran, ten, lay on the divan with a comic. "I'll do my maths when I'm in the mood," he told his mother Parul. She raised an eyebrow but said nothing. At six, he fed the fish. At seven, he watched his neighbour's kite from the balcony. At eight, he opened the book, stared at the fractions and closed it again. "Not in the mood yet." At half past nine Parul sat beside him. "Kiran, does the mood usually come before or after you start?" He thought. "After, I think." "Then let's start." Ten sums later, he was grumbling but moving, and in bed by half past ten.

qa.q: What did Kiran do at six?
qa.a: At six, he fed the fish.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling each time he closed the maths book?
qa.a: He felt reluctant and unmotivated, waiting for a mood to arrive before starting.

qa.q: What did Parul's question help Kiran see?
qa.a: It helped him see for himself that the mood usually comes after starting, not before, so he could begin without it.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul to watch Kiran drift through the evening?
qa.a: Parul seems patient but concerned, choosing to wait and then ask a question rather than nag.

grounding: Illustrates a child putting off homework until he feels like it, and drifting through the evening.

passage:
Tejas: "Shalini, it's seven. Homework?"
Shalini: "Later, Papa. I don't feel like it yet."
Tejas: "When do you think you'll feel like it?"
Shalini: "I don't know. Soon."
Tejas: "Yesterday you said soon, and you finished at eleven."
Shalini: "Yesterday was different. The chapter was boring."
Tejas: "Is today's chapter exciting?"
Shalini: "...No."
Tejas: "So the feeling might not come?"
Shalini: "Ugh. Maybe."
Tejas: "Try this. Open the book and read the first question aloud. That's all."
Shalini: "Just one question?"
Tejas: "Just one."
(She reads it. Then the second. At eight-thirty she closes the book, done.)
Shalini: "That was sneaky, Papa."

qa.q: What time did Shalini finish the night before?
qa.a: She finished at eleven.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about starting homework at seven?
qa.a: She felt unmotivated and reluctant, waiting to feel like it, even though she couldn't say when that would be.

qa.q: Which step helped Shalini get going?
qa.a: Reading just the first question aloud gave her a tiny start, and once she began she kept going until she finished.

qa.q: How does Tejas approach his daughter's delay?
qa.a: Tejas stays calm and asks questions, reminding her of last night instead of scolding, then offers a very small first step.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child waiting to feel like doing homework and a parent helping her see that the feeling comes after starting.

passage:
Monday. Pankaj, sixteen, had a chemistry test on Friday. Every time he thought of the thick textbook, his chest tightened. He cleaned his room instead. Then his cycle.
Wednesday. His sister Bhavna put a timer on his desk. "Ten minutes. Then you can stop." He sat, heart heavy, and opened chapter four. The first three minutes were awful. By minute eight he was drawing a table of elements. When the timer rang, he kept going for another forty minutes.
Thursday. He sat down straight after dinner, still with a small flutter of dread. It lasted two minutes this time. "It's only the door that's heavy," he told Bhavna.

qa.q: On which day was Pankaj's chemistry test?
qa.a: The test was on Friday.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling on Monday when he thought of the textbook?
qa.a: He felt dread, with his chest tightening, so he cleaned his room and cycle instead.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna's timer work?
qa.a: Committing to only ten minutes got Pankaj past the hardest first minutes, and once he was in, the resistance faded.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Pankaj says the door is the heavy part?
qa.a: Bhavna would likely feel pleased and proud that her small timer trick helped her brother see how starting works.

grounding: Shows across days a teenager whose dread of revising is mostly about the first minutes, fading once he starts.

passage: Indu, come, sit. You think your mother Nirmala was always the studious one? At fifteen, she hated opening her geography book. I'm your Nani; I watched it every evening. She'd sit, sigh, move the book, sharpen three pencils, fetch water. The dread was all over her face. One evening I said, "Just read to me for ten minutes. I'll be shelling peas." She grumbled and began with the chapter on rivers. After ten minutes I said she could stop. She didn't. She read until the peas were done and then asked me to quiz her. Later she told me, "The first few minutes are the worst, Nani. After that it's just work."

qa.q: What was Nani doing while Nirmala read aloud?
qa.a: Nani was shelling peas.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling before she began reading?
qa.a: She felt dread and resistance, sighing and sharpening pencils to delay opening the book.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Nirmala start?
qa.a: Nani's invitation to read aloud for just ten minutes made the entrance small, and after that the resistance faded.

qa.q: How did Nani see Nirmala's pencil sharpening and water fetching?
qa.a: Nani saw them as ways of putting off the dreaded first minutes, not as laziness, and offered a gentle way in.

grounding: An elder tells how a teenager dreaded opening her book, but once reading for ten minutes, the resistance faded.

passage: The wedding band next door started at six, and Darshan, fifteen, had a history mock the next morning. He lay on his bed, staring at the ceiling. The thought of revising felt like climbing a wall. "I can't with this noise," he told his cousin Salma, who was visiting. She handed him her spare earplugs. "Ten minutes. Just the first page." He groaned, but opened the book to the Mughals and started reading, the drums thudding through the wall. The first few minutes felt like wading through mud. Then he was underlining. When Salma looked in an hour later, he waved her away without looking up.

qa.q: What was the history mock about that Darshan opened to?
qa.a: He opened the book to the Mughals.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling as he lay staring at the ceiling?
qa.a: He felt dread and heaviness, as if revising were a wall to climb, and used the noise as a reason not to begin.

qa.q: What helped Darshan past the hardest part?
qa.a: Salma's earplugs and her suggestion of just ten minutes on the first page got him through the start, after which he kept going.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when Darshan waves her away?
qa.a: Salma might feel amused and pleased, seeing that the cousin who couldn't start was now too absorbed to talk.

grounding: Shows a teenager dreading revision in a noisy house, whose resistance fades once the book has been open for a few minutes.

passage:
Tutor's note, Saturday batch, Class 10.
Pallavi has been stuck on her English essay for two weeks. Each week she says she will start "when I have a full hour". Today I tried something different. I asked her to write only one sentence, any sentence, and said she could stop after five minutes if she wanted. She looked doubtful but agreed. She wrote the first line, then the second. At the five-minute mark I reminded her she could stop. She shook her head and kept going. By the end of class she had a full paragraph. Her classmate Jatin asked to try the same trick next week. I will start each session this way.

qa.q: How long had Pallavi been stuck on her essay?
qa.a: Pallavi had been stuck for two weeks.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when asked to write one sentence?
qa.a: She felt doubtful at first, but the promise that she could stop made starting feel safe.

qa.q: Why did the five-minute rule work for Pallavi?
qa.a: Committing to one sentence and permission to stop removed the pressure, and once she was moving she chose to keep going.

qa.q: How might Jatin be affected by seeing Pallavi's paragraph?
qa.a: Jatin seems curious and hopeful, asking to try the same trick next week.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a teenager using a five-minute, one-sentence start with permission to stop, and gaining momentum.

passage:
Dear Diary, Wed.
Maths assignment due Friday and I've avoided it since Monday. Tonight Madhuri told me her trick on the phone: "Say you'll do five minutes. Just lay out the book, the pencil, the ruler. If you hate it after five, stop."
I felt silly doing it. Set the timer on the kitchen clock. Opened to exercise 7. Did question 1. Timer rang. I was halfway through question 2, and it felt dumb to stop in the middle. So I didn't. Finished 6 questions!! 😊
The weird part: I wasn't more motivated when I started. I got motivated after.
Trying it again tomorrow.
Ayesha

qa.q: Which exercise did Ayesha open to?
qa.a: Ayesha opened to exercise 7.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel about trying the five-minute trick?
qa.a: Ayesha felt silly at first, but ended up pleased and surprised after finishing six questions.

qa.q: Why did the five-minute rule work for Ayesha?
qa.a: It asked only for a tiny start with permission to stop, and once in motion, stopping mid-question felt harder than continuing.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel hearing that the trick worked?
qa.a: Madhuri would probably feel glad and a little proud that her advice helped her friend finally start the assignment.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows committing to five minutes and laying out tools, with motion creating momentum.

passage:
Sunday, 11 pm.
Thesis chapter 2 still not started. Today's reasons: the desk was covered in laundry, and by the time I cleared it, it was 3 pm, which is "not a full day". Yesterday the reason was a headache. Last week, Gurpreet was visiting and I needed "the right mood".
I keep waiting for a morning where my desk is clean, my head is clear and I have eight free hours. It has never happened. Not once in two months.
Gurpreet said something before leaving: "You're not waiting for conditions. You're waiting to not be scared." That stung.
Tomorrow: 9 am, messy desk, one paragraph. Whatever mood I'm in.
Nikita

qa.q: What was covering Nikita's desk on Sunday?
qa.a: The desk was covered in laundry.

qa.q: How did Nikita feel about Gurpreet's comment?
qa.a: It stung; Nikita felt hurt but also recognised the truth that the waiting was about fear.

qa.q: What plan does Nikita make, and why could it work?
qa.a: Starting at 9 am with a messy desk and just one paragraph drops the demand for perfect conditions, which never arrive.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have seen the visit and the unstarted chapter?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems to have noticed that the reasons kept changing and guessed that fear, not conditions, was the real block.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult waiting for a clear desk, a full day and the right mood before starting a thesis chapter.

passage: Damini, twenty-two, was writing a dissertation on water use for her college in Satara while living at home in the village. The chapter on farmers' interviews was due in a month. She told herself she needed the right setup: the electricity steady, the courtyard quiet, the whole day free. Every morning something broke the picture: the buffalo needed feeding, a neighbour came by, the power went off. Her friend Ankita, a schoolteacher, visited one afternoon and found her sorting pens. "Write in the noise," Ankita said. "I correct forty notebooks with children shouting." Damini laughed, then sat on the step with her notebook. She wrote a page by lamplight that evening.

qa.q: What was Damini's dissertation about?
qa.a: It was a dissertation on water use.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when Ankita found her sorting pens?
qa.a: She felt stuck and a bit defensive, still waiting for a quiet, full day that never came.

qa.q: Which choice finally helped Damini start?
qa.a: Sitting on the step and writing despite the noise and the lamp, instead of waiting for steady electricity and a free day.

qa.q: How does Ankita see the wait for perfect conditions?
qa.a: Ankita, who corrects notebooks amid children's shouting, sees it as unnecessary and encourages Damini to write anyway.

grounding: Shows a young adult waiting for ideal conditions to start a dissertation chapter, until she writes despite the noise.

passage:
Disha: "Yusuf, you've had the same email draft open since Monday."
Yusuf: "I'll send it. I just can't get going lately."
Disha: "Lately meaning how long?"
Yusuf: "A few weeks. Maybe more. Everything feels flat. I sleep ten hours and I'm still tired."
Disha: "You used to love your running club."
Yusuf: "Haven't gone in a month. It's not laziness, I promise. I just... can't make myself care."
Disha: "I believe you. This doesn't sound like you being lazy. It sounds heavy."
Yusuf: "So what, I just push harder?"
Disha: "No. I think it's worth talking to a doctor or a counsellor about it. Would you let me help you book something today?"
Yusuf: (quiet) "Okay. Today."
Disha: "I'll sit with you while you call."

qa.q: How long had Yusuf's email draft been open?
qa.a: It had been open since Monday.

qa.q: Why does Disha keep asking Yusuf how long it has lasted?
qa.a: Disha is worried and concerned, checking whether this is a passing slump or something deeper, and names it as heavy rather than lazy.

qa.q: What did Disha do well?
qa.a: Disha listened, did not lecture about discipline, gently suggested a doctor or counsellor and offered to sit with Yusuf during the call that same day.

qa.q: What is it like for Yusuf to hear that it doesn't sound like laziness?
qa.a: Yusuf likely feels relieved and understood, having worried that people would see it as laziness.

passage: I'm Arohi, and I shared a flat with Rajni for two years. She was the one who organised everything: rent, groceries, weekend trips. Last winter I noticed her laptop open to the same job application for days. Dishes piled up in her room, which was never like her. She stopped coming to our Sunday dosa breakfast. When I asked, she said, "I can't start anything. I'm just tired." It had been over a month. I didn't give her a pep talk; I'd have hated that. I sat on her bed and said, "This seems bigger than being tired. Would you see a counsellor? I can find one near us." She nodded. We looked one up together that evening.

qa.q: What breakfast did Rajni stop coming to?
qa.a: Rajni stopped coming to the Sunday dosa breakfast.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when noticing the change in Rajni?
qa.a: Arohi felt worried and concerned, seeing that this was not like Rajni and had gone on for over a month.

qa.q: What was wise about Arohi's response?
qa.a: Arohi skipped the pep talk, named the change kindly, suggested a counsellor and helped look one up that same evening.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when Arohi sits on her bed and offers to help?
qa.a: Rajni might feel relieved and cared for, since someone noticed without blaming her for being unable to start.

grounding: A flatmate notices weeks of being unable to start anything and gently suggests a counsellor rather than lecturing.

passage:
Team lead's note, private, Tuesday.
Jatin has missed three small deadlines this month. This is unusual; for two years he was the first to volunteer. In meetings he stares at his screen, and he told me today that he "just can't get started on anything, even things I like". He said it has been going on for about six weeks and that he feels flat most days. I did not talk about performance targets. I told him I'd noticed, that I was concerned for him, not the work, and I gave him the details for our staff counselling service and suggested he also see his doctor. He booked a counselling slot for Thursday while I was there. I will check in with him on Friday.
Siddharth

qa.q: How many deadlines had Jatin missed this month?
qa.a: Jatin had missed three small deadlines.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel about the change in Jatin?
qa.a: Siddharth seems concerned and caring, focusing on Jatin's wellbeing rather than the missed work.

qa.q: What steps did Siddharth take, and why were they helpful?
qa.a: Siddharth avoided talking about targets, shared the counselling service details, suggested a doctor, stayed while Jatin booked a slot and planned a Friday check-in.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jatin to hear someone say they are concerned for him, not the work?
qa.a: Jatin might feel relieved and less ashamed, since the flatness was treated as something real rather than a discipline problem.

grounding: A team lead notices a worker unable to start anything for weeks and points him to counselling and a doctor instead of lecturing.

passage: Zanele was a junior architect in Johannesburg, and Thursdays were her flattest days. She didn't feel like drawing anything. Her colleague Chidi, who had been at the firm for six years, once asked her why she still started at eight sharp on those days. She shrugged. "Because if I wait until I feel like it, I'll start at three." Her routine never changed: coffee, open yesterday's drawing, fix one small line, then the next. By ten, most Thursdays, she was absorbed. Some days the drive never came, and she still finished her list. "Motivation shows up late," she told Chidi. "I've stopped waiting for it at the door."

qa.q: What time did Zanele start work on flat days?
qa.a: She started at eight sharp.

qa.q: How does Zanele feel on Thursdays at first?
qa.a: She feels flat and unmotivated, not wanting to draw anything.

qa.q: What does Zanele's routine show about getting going on flat days?
qa.a: Fixing one small line in yesterday's drawing at the same time every day lets action come first, so motivation often follows by ten.

qa.q: How might Chidi see Zanele's approach?
qa.a: Chidi, after six years at the firm, might recognise it as a mature habit and respect her for starting even without drive.

grounding: Shows an experienced worker starting at a fixed time on flat days, treating motivation as something that follows action.

passage: At the government school where Madhav taught Class 8 science, Mondays were hard. He'd sleep badly, the bus would be crowded, and some weeks he felt nothing for the lesson. Kashish, a first-year teacher, asked him in the staffroom how he always looked prepared. Madhav showed her his routine card: "7:45 arrive. 7:50 write today's aim on the board. 7:55 set out materials. 8:00 first question to class." "Even when you don't feel like it?" "Especially then. Once the aim is on the board, my hands know the rest." Kashish tried it the next Monday. By the second period she noticed she had forgotten to feel tired.

qa.q: What does Madhav do at 7:50?
qa.a: At 7:50 he writes today's aim on the board.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel by the second period on Monday?
qa.a: She felt more energetic, surprised to find she had forgotten to feel tired.

qa.q: Why does Madhav's routine card help on flat days?
qa.a: It removes the need to feel motivated first: each small fixed step leads to the next, so action builds the drive.

qa.q: How might Madhav's students experience his routine on flat days?
qa.a: They get a clear aim and a prepared lesson every day, without noticing whether their teacher felt like it.

grounding: Shows an experienced teacher keeping a fixed routine on flat days, with motivation following action.

passage:
Dear Irfan,

You asked how I keep writing the weekly report even when I'd rather not. Honestly, I rarely feel like it. Most Mondays I sit down feeling heavy and a little bored.

Here's what I do. At 9:30, whatever my mood, I open last week's report and copy the headings. Then I fill in the easiest number. Then the next. By ten, I'm usually interested. And on the days I'm not, the report still gets done, because the routine doesn't ask how I'm feeling.

I used to think I needed motivation to start. Now I think starting is what makes it.

See you at lunch,
Kunal

How does Kunal usually feel on Monday mornings?
qa.a: Kunal usually feels heavy and a little bored, rarely feeling like writing the report.

qa.q: What could Irfan copy from Kunal's routine?

qa.q: How might Irfan see Kunal after reading the letter?

passage: Nazia, listen, your Bua, Parul, was just like you at nine. Her teacher gave the class two weeks to make a model of a village well. Two weeks! To her, that was forever. I'm your Dadi and her mother, and I remember her saying, "There's so much time, Amma, I'll do it next week." Next week became "after Sunday". Then, on the second-last evening, she came running to me in tears. No clay, no straws, and the shop was closing. We ran together in the rain. She stayed up late pressing wet clay while I held the torch. The well leaned to one side. She still keeps a photo of that crooked well.

qa.q: How did Dadi experience Parul's last-minute rush?
qa.a: Dadi ran through the rain to the shop and held the torch late into the night, supporting Parul through a rush that could have been avoided.

grounding: An elder tells how a child given two weeks for a project felt there was endless time and did nothing until the last evenings.

passage: In their Kochi apartment, Thomas, eleven, had a two-week deadline for a scrapbook on local birds. His mother pinned the date on the fridge. "Plenty of time," he said, and went cycling with his neighbour Ishita every evening. The fridge note became part of the wallpaper. On the Friday before the Monday deadline, Ishita mentioned she had pasted her last picture. Thomas froze. He had four photos and no captions. All weekend he worked, cutting and writing, while Ishita cycled alone. On Sunday night he finished, eyes gritty. "Two weeks felt like forever," he told his mother, "until it was two days."

qa.q: What was Thomas's scrapbook about?
qa.a: It was a scrapbook on local birds.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Ishita mentioned her last picture?
qa.a: He froze, feeling shocked and panicky, realising he had only four photos and no captions.

qa.q: What could help Thomas next time a deadline seems far away?
qa.a: Breaking it into small tasks with dates, such as photos in week one and captions in week two, so the distant deadline feels real sooner.

qa.q: What is it like for Ishita when Thomas has to work all weekend?
qa.a: Ishita ends up cycling alone, missing her friend while he rushes to catch up.

grounding: Shows a child feeling there is endless time for a two-week project until only the last two days remain.

passage: At eleven at night in the boarding-school hostel, Samir, sixteen, was still typing his physics lab report due at 8 a.m. The corridor lights were off; he worked by the glow of his laptop. Maria ma'am, the house warden, had done her last round at ten and told him to sleep soon. At two, Samir printed the pages in the common room, graphs slightly crooked. He felt a rush, almost pride. "I work best like this," he whispered to himself. At eight he submitted it, eyes burning. His teacher returned it a week later: "Good ideas, careless graphs, conclusion missing." Samir stared at the red ink and felt the rush drain out of him.

qa.q: When was Samir's physics lab report due?
qa.a: It was due at 8 a.m.

qa.q: What did Samir feel when he printed the pages at two?
qa.a: He felt a rush, almost pride, believing he works best under pressure.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The late-night rush left the graphs careless and the conclusion missing; starting a few days earlier would leave time to check.

passage:
Dear Sachin,

You asked how the geography project went. Honestly? I did the whole thing last night. Started at nine, finished at four in the morning. Maps, write-up, everything. And I felt amazing at three, like some kind of genius. The coffee, the silence, the panic, it all made me fast.

Then this morning I read it on the bus and saw I'd labelled the Ganga as the Yamuna. Twice. And half the write-up was one long paragraph. I got a C.

I keep telling myself I'm a pressure person. But maybe I only feel clever at 3 a.m. because I'm too tired to notice the mistakes.

Your cousin,
Hrithik

qa.a: Hrithik got a C.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel at three in the morning?
qa.a: Hrithik felt amazing, like a genius, fuelled by coffee, silence and panic.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try for the next project?
qa.a: Start a few days earlier and keep one calm evening to check the work, so errors like mixing up the rivers are caught.

qa.q: How might Sachin respond to this letter?
qa.a: Sachin might feel sympathetic and a little amused, and could encourage Hrithik to test starting earlier next time.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows working frantically the night before, feeling the adrenaline as ability, and delivering rushed work.

passage: Want to know my worst school habit? I'm Rajni, and in Class Eleven I lived for the night before. My friend Nandini would start projects a week early, and I'd tease her. "Where's the thrill?" The thrill for me was midnight: heart racing, fingers flying, the feeling that I could pull anything off. And I did pull things off, sort of. My biology file went in with smudged diagrams and a missing index. I slept three hours and fell asleep in the practical exam the next day. My teacher said, "You're capable, but I'm marking what's on the page." That line stayed with me. The rush felt like talent. The page said otherwise.

qa.q: How many hours did Rajni sleep before the practical exam?
qa.a: Rajni slept three hours.

qa.q: What did Rajni feel at midnight while working on projects?
qa.a: Rajni felt thrilled and excited, heart racing, sure of being able to pull anything off.

qa.q: What would you advise Rajni based on the teacher's comment?
qa.a: Start earlier like Nandini, so that the work on the page matches the ability, instead of relying on the midnight rush.

qa.q: How might Nandini have seen Rajni's teasing?
qa.a: Nandini may have found it mildly annoying but stayed calm, trusting her own early-start habit.

grounding: A teenager tells how the adrenaline of night-before work felt like ability but produced rushed, weaker results.

passage: Samir, twenty, always said he worked best under pressure. His marketing case study, worth a third of the term grade, was due on Friday at noon. He planned to write it on Thursday night, as always. On Wednesday evening, he got a fever. By Thursday he could barely sit up. His roommate Shankar brought him soup and asked, "Should I email the professor?" Samir shook his head. "I'll manage tonight." He managed four hundred words of the three thousand before his eyes closed. Shankar emailed the professor anyway, with Samir's permission, the next morning. The professor granted two days, but docked ten percent for late notice.

qa.q: How much of the term grade was the case study worth?
qa.a: It was worth a third of the term grade.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he shook his head at Shankar?
qa.a: He felt stubborn and still hopeful, clinging to the belief that he could manage under pressure even while ill.

qa.q: What went wrong with Samir's approach?
qa.a: Leaving everything to the last night left no room for a surprise like a fever, so he lost marks for late notice.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel watching Samir struggle?
qa.a: Shankar seems worried and caring, bringing soup and wanting to email the professor early to protect Samir.

grounding: Shows a student who claims to work best under pressure and leaves things to the last day, until illness breaks the plan.

passage: In a Pune college canteen, Hafsa stirred her tea. "I'm a last-minute person," she told her friend Hansa. "My brain only works under pressure." Hansa, who planned everything, raised an eyebrow. "How did the economics project go?" "B plus. Fine." "You could have got an A. You told me you skipped the last section." Hafsa shrugged, but her smile slipped. She thought of the three nights that month she'd slept four hours, the headache that had followed her through the week, the typo in her title. "It works," she said, less sure now. "Sometimes." Hansa pushed a sticky note across the table: "Start dates?" Hafsa picked it up.

qa.q: What grade did Hafsa get on the economics project?
qa.a: She got a B plus.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's smile slipping suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and less sure, remembering the lost sleep, headache and typo that the rush had cost.

qa.q: What small step could help Hafsa use the sticky note?
qa.a: She could write a start date for each upcoming project, a few days before the deadline, and keep the last day for checking.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Hafsa's claim about pressure?
qa.a: Hansa, who plans everything, sees it as costing Hafsa marks and sleep, and gently challenges it.

grounding: Shows a student who says she works best under pressure beginning to see the cost to quality and sleep.

passage:
Week one. Bidisha, twenty-one, had a sociology term paper due on the 30th. This time she wrote two dates of her own on the calendar: rough draft by the 18th, full draft by the 24th. Her friend Santosh laughed. "Fake deadlines?"
Week two. On the 17th she typed a messy, ugly draft, full of notes like "fix this". It felt strange to be done early with something bad.
Week three. On the 22nd, the library's online database went down for two days. Santosh panicked about his paper. Bidisha shrugged; her sources were already in. She spent the last week trimming paragraphs and fixing references, and submitted on the 29th, calm.

qa.q: By what date did Bidisha plan her rough draft?
qa.a: Rough draft by the 18th.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when the library database went down?
qa.a: She felt calm and unbothered, since her sources were already in.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha's own dates help her?
qa.a: Finishing a rough draft early left room for surprises like the database outage, so the last week was for improving, not scrambling.

qa.q: How was Santosh affected by the database going down?
qa.a: Santosh panicked, because unlike Bidisha, he still needed the sources for his paper.

grounding: Shows over weeks a student setting personal milestones before the real date and using the final days to improve.

passage: Seema, you're starting your first job, so let me tell you about Pallavi, my classmate from nursing college in Madurai, years ago. I'm your Periamma; I was there. Our case studies were due every month on the last Friday. Pallavi always wrote her own date in the corner of her notebook: the Friday before. "The college's date is for the college," she'd say. "Mine is for me." One month, a flood closed the college hostel for four days right before the deadline. Half of us lost our notes and scrambled. Pallavi had a rough draft done already. She spent those days polishing it at her aunt's house and got the highest mark.

qa.q: What date did Pallavi write in the corner of her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote the Friday before the college's deadline.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when the flood closed the hostel?
qa.a: She was likely calm and secure, knowing her rough draft was already done while others scrambled.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference for Pallavi?
qa.a: Setting her own deadline a week early, so when the flood struck she only had to polish, not start.

qa.q: How did the flood affect the other students in the story?
qa.a: Half of the class lost their notes and had to scramble, stressed, right before the deadline.

grounding: An elder tells of a student who set her own earlier deadline and so had room when a surprise flood hit.

On her day off, she tidied the charts and the introduction, and submitted on the 19th.
